# Biological plausibility: do the model's drivers point the way physiology says?

**Research prototype. Not a medical device, not for clinical use.** Generated by `python -m src.eval.plausibility`.

For each input with a known physiological direction, the Spearman correlation between the input's value and its exact TreeSHAP contribution on onset windows. A positive rho means a higher value makes the model raise the risk. Verdict: *agrees* when the sign matches physiology, *little effect* when |rho| < 0.1. *Attention* is the input's share of the model's mean absolute contribution.

**15 of 17 inputs with a learned direction point the way physiology predicts; they carry 99% of the model's attention among the checked inputs** (1 with little effect).

| Mean glucose, last hour | higher lowers risk | glucose running lower is closer to 70 | +0.30 | 0.4% | DISAGREES |
| Glucose trend, last 30 min | higher lowers risk | a falling trend (negative slope) raises the risk | -0.84 | 2.2% | agrees |
| Glucose trend, last 60 min | higher lowers risk | a falling trend raises the risk | -0.79 | 2.3% | agrees |
| Change over last 15 min | higher lowers risk | a recent drop raises the risk | -0.79 | 0.9% | agrees |
| Last reading below 70 | higher lowers risk | a recent low weakens counter-regulation, so a longer gap lowers the risk | -0.09 | 0.6% | little effect |
| Time below 70, 6 h | higher raises risk | more recent time below 70 raises the risk | +0.36 | 0.5% | agrees |
| Steps, last hour | higher raises risk | activity takes up glucose without insulin | +0.38 | 0.3% | agrees |

## Why some inputs disagree

The inputs the models rely on most (current glucose, the recent fall, the sulfonylurea dose, HbA1c) all agree. The disagreements are small inputs, and they have two known causes:

* **Overlapping inputs share the credit.** Several inputs describe the same thing (the last 15-minute change, the 30-minute and 60-minute slopes; the current level and the hourly mean). The model leans on one of them and uses the others as small corrections, which can carry the opposite sign. Read the group, not the single input: the main trend input agrees in every model.
* **Confounding by indication.** In the synthetic data, patients on higher sulfonylurea doses also run higher glucose (the dose was raised because control was poor), so the dose looks like it *raises* the risk of a high. That is how the patients were treated, not what the drug does. The same applies to diabetes duration and lows.
* **Post-meal timing.** A large rise in the last 3 hours often means the peak has passed and glucose is coming down, so the model lowers the risk of a high after it. That is physiologically reasonable.

**Possible fix:** LightGBM can enforce a physiological direction for chosen inputs (monotone constraints). Training with constraints on the key drivers would make every explanation point the right way; its cost in accuracy has to be measured before adopting it.

## Reading this

* **Synthetic model:** the simulator was built from these mechanisms (docs/model_card.md), so agreement there is expected and partly by construction. It shows the model learned the intended biology, not that the biology holds in real patients.
* **Real-patient model:** it sees only CGM and time of day, so only CGM-derived drivers can be checked. These are learned from real patients and are the meaningful test.
* **What this does not show:** SHAP explains the model, not the patient. A driver that agrees with physiology is consistent with known biology; it is not proof that this mechanism caused a given low.
* Literature behind each mechanism: sulfonylureas close beta-cell KATP channels and release insulin regardless of glucose; contracting muscle takes up glucose via GLUT4 without insulin and stays insulin-sensitive for hours; recent and repeated lows blunt glucagon and adrenaline counter-regulation; reduced kidney function prolongs sulfonylurea and insulin action. See the finals feedback document's literature map for sources.
